text: Lessons 5 and 6 built the real mechanism: typed, directional relationships in cmdb_rel_ci, visible as a graph through the Dependency View. Impact analysis simply uses that graph for its actual purpose — answering, if this CI goes down, what else is affected, by starting at the failed CI and walking its relationships outward through every CI that depends on it.

This only works if the relationships feeding the query are accurate. Impact analysis built on missing or backward relationships produces a confident, wrong answer, which is worse than no answer at all, because people will act on that wrong answer as though it were reliably true.

A common mistake is checking only the CIs directly related to the failed one and stopping there. Real environments are rarely one hop deep. Transitive impact means following depends-on relationships through multiple hops until you reach the business services and applications that real people actually notice when they stop working.

Picture a database server scheduled for emergency maintenance. Querying its relationship graph shows the application server depends on it; that application server runs the Order Processing application; and Order Processing, per its own separate relationship, supports the Online Ordering business service.

Follow that full chain, and the honest answer to what's affected isn't a database server — it's the Online Ordering business service, and everyone who relies on placing orders through it. That's the level of impact a business stakeholder, not just an infrastructure team, actually needs to hear.

This isn't abstract. A later course in this path builds Change Risk Assessment and CAB Conflict Detection, and both features are, underneath, running this exact impact-analysis graph walk. If the relationships are missing, backward, or stale, those features will confidently miscalculate risk and silently miss real conflicts. Next: a worked lab tracing exactly this kind of chain by hand.
